sentences: Good question, and it's the payoff of the whole design.

That randomness is what keeps two candidates from splitting the vote again and again.

With consistent hashing, both the servers and the keys are placed on the same ring, and each key belongs to the first server you meet going clockwise.
When a server joins or leaves, only the keys next to it move, instead of nearly everything being reshuffled.
What do you think happens to the load if one server gets only a single spot on the ring?
That's a fair way to put it, but there's a subtle catch.
During a network partition, a system has to choose between answering every request and keeping all the replicas in agreement.
Neither choice is wrong, because it depends on whether a stale answer or no answer costs you more.
Which would you pick for a shopping cart, and why?
Let's think about what happens when a worker dies halfway through a job.
The master notices that the worker stopped answering its pings, so it marks the worker's tasks as idle and hands them to someone else.
That works because map and reduce tasks are deterministic, so running one twice gives the same output.
Can you see why a task that gave different answers each time would break this?
Good, that's the right instinct.
Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer, and Docker reuses a layer from its cache as long as nothing above it has changed.
So if you copy your source code before installing the dependencies, every small edit forces a full reinstall.

Right, and that's exactly where Kafka gets its throughput.
A topic is split into partitions, and within a consumer group each partition is read by only one consumer at a time.
Adding more consumers than partitions doesn't help, because the extra ones just sit idle.
So what limits the parallelism of your service here?
Hold on, the average can hide a lot here.
If ninety nine requests take ten milliseconds and one takes two seconds, the mean still looks healthy, while one user in a hundred is waiting far too long.
That's why we look at the slowest one percent of requests, and why queues can build up long before the servers look busy.
What would you measure next in your load test?
Let's walk through your goroutines one at a time.
A WaitGroup is just a counter, so you add one before launching each goroutine, call Done when it finishes, and Wait blocks until the counter hits zero.
If you call Add inside the goroutine itself, the main function might reach Wait before any goroutine has registered.
Where would you move that call?

Terraform keeps a state file that maps the resources in your configuration to the real ones in the cloud, and it plans changes by comparing the two.
If two people apply at the same time without locking, the state can get corrupted or silently overwritten.
How would you store that file so a whole team can share it safely?
Good catch, retries are where this gets interesting.
A request is idempotent if sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once, which is why updating a record is safe to retry but creating one might produce duplicates.
Clients usually fix that by sending a unique key, so the server can recognize a repeat and return the first result.
What would your service do if it saw the same key twice?
